header.scope: Lost: the contract was split and the contested international business went to local acquiring; per the rep, the US stayed with us.
header.tag_why: Stefan needed his own approval numbers by market for his CFO ("I can't take an average to my CFO"), and we answered with an average uplift while our customer-specific analysis landed only after Adyen's country-level test was finished.

evidence.excerpt: A new head of payments. Stefan. They'd never had one.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: the first thing he did was pull declines by country.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: A few of their international markets looked bad to him.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I knew the engineering manager had left. I didn't know they'd hired a head of payments.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: No competitor started this. A new payments owner ran his own decline cut by country and found international markets he didn't like. We had the same data and never showed it to him. We didn't even know he existed, so the evaluation was framed entirely in his analysis, which the rep never saw. This was a renewal that went unwatched after the champion left, not a competitive bake-off that started from scratch.
trigger.messaging: Lead international accounts with a proactive, customer-specific approvals-by-country view so that M1's "grow globally, in every currency" is backed by their own numbers before a new owner pulls them himself.

evidence.excerpt: Stefan recommended it and the CFO approved.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: this went to the CFO two weeks ago.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I can't take an average to my CFO.
evidence.label: quote

decider.insight: Stefan built the case and the CFO signed off, so the real audience for our proof was a CFO. The transcript gives no sign we ever reached the CFO. The rep heard about the CFO step only after it had happened, which means we were reporting on the decision, not taking part in it.
decider.messaging: Give the payments lead a CFO-ready, per-market business case in money terms (his "money left on the table"), not a product deck with an average uplift.

evidence.excerpt: Adyen ran a test on a slice of their international traffic and came back with results by country.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: local acquiring
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I can't tell you what the test showed. He wouldn't share it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: They got very specific. What's our approval rate in this country, on this card type, by issuer. And why.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: Adyen won on method, and we don't know whether they won on results. They ran a live test on his traffic and reported back by country, which is exactly the format Stefan then demanded from us, down to card type and issuer. After that test, "local acquiring" became his frame, and the rep says she had no counter to it.
competitor.messaging: Build a local-acquiring answer for international accounts that offers a test or analysis on the customer's own traffic, reported by country, card type and issuer with reasons, because that is the bar the competitor set.

evidence.excerpt: The Authorization Boost deck. The average uplift customers see.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: that's an average. What's mine?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I offered a roadmap session and he didn't take it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: He said it was the most useful thing we'd sent him.
evidence.label: fact

message.insight: The rep says "we weren't really pitching," but we did pitch: M4's average uplift. It was dismissed outright, and the roadmap offer was declined. The only thing that landed was the custom analysis of his own data, which arrived too late. The rep's evidence for product love (developers, billing) is her own read, and nothing in the transcript ties it to anything Stefan said.
message.messaging: Retire the average-uplift line (M4) as an opener with payments leaders and replace it with "here are your approvals by market, and what we'd fix".

evidence.excerpt: I don't think there was a moment. It was kind of decided before we got in the room.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: But that landed three weeks after he asked, and by then the test was finished.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Real findings. Things we could have fixed.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: When the renewal notice went out and Stefan replied asking to split the contract.
evidence.label: fact

decided.insight: The rep's claim that there was no moment and nothing to do conflicts with her own account. The window was the three weeks between Stefan's request and our analysis, and Adyen's test finished inside that window. The analysis found fixable issues, by the rep's account, so the loss looks like a timing and access failure, not a decision that was fixed in advance. The exact order of the CFO approval and our analysis delivery is unclear.
decided.messaging: Make "your numbers within days, not weeks" an explicit commitment in competitive renewals, because a late analysis that the customer calls useful still loses to a test that is already finished.

evidence.excerpt: A market-by-market view of their own approval rates, with reasons.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: He asked who at Stripe looks at his numbers every month, and I didn't have a name.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Before I took the account. So nine months? Ten.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: There were two gaps, and neither was a missing feature. The first was speed in turning around his own approval data. The second was the lack of a named person who owns his numbers every month. With no business review in roughly nine or ten months, the second gap was real. M5's tiered response times answer a support question Stefan never asked.
gaps.messaging: Reposition M5 from response-time tiers to a named person who reviews your approvals by market every month, for accounts with international volume.

evidence.excerpt: Money left on the table.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Local cards, local rails.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: He doesn't say "authorization," he says "approvals."
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I heard from Stripe when I said I was leaving.
evidence.label: quote

language.insight: His problem was lost revenue ("money left on the table"), described in approvals and local rails. We described it in authorization rates, ML features and averages. His line about hearing from Stripe only when he said he was leaving is a direct verdict on our coverage, and it undercuts the rep's description of the account as healthy.
language.messaging: Rewrite acceptance messaging in the buyer's words: approvals, by market, money left on the table, and drop "authorization" and "average" from the headline.

gaps.question: Which markets looked bad, and what did Stefan's decline analysis show?
gaps.follow_up: Elena: ask Stefan for the markets and numbers behind his decline-by-country review (Brazil and which European markets?), and have the payments performance team map them against their own analysis.

gaps.question: What did Adyen's test show?
gaps.follow_up: Elena: ask Stefan whether he will share even the headline per-country approval deltas from the test.

gaps.question: When did the deal turn, and what happened right before?
gaps.follow_up: Elena: give a dated timeline covering the renewal notice, the split request, Stefan's ask for the market view, the end of Adyen's test, the CFO approval, and the delivery of our analysis.

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got a positive reaction?
gaps.follow_up: Elena: besides the late analysis, did anything we said or showed get a positive reaction from Stefan, and did he say anything specific about developers or billing?

gaps.question: Did anyone from our side ever meet or present to the CFO?
gaps.follow_up: Elena: did we have any contact with the CFO, and what did the CFO see from us?

gaps.question: Which provider and which markets actually moved, and is the move confirmed?
gaps.follow_up: Elena: confirm whether the international traffic went to Adyen, which markets moved, and what share of volume stayed with us.

gaps.question: Why did the market-by-market analysis take three weeks?
gaps.follow_up: Payments performance team: what drove the turnaround time, and what would it take to deliver this within days for an at-risk renewal?

gaps.question: Is there a win-back path using the fixable findings?
gaps.follow_up: Elena: ask Stefan whether fixing the issues the analysis found could reopen any of the markets that moved.

close.rep_takeaway: When the person who bought us leaves, treat the account as at risk and find the new owner before the renewal notice does it for you. When a payments leader asks "what's mine," get his own numbers in front of him fast: the analysis he called the most useful thing we'd sent arrived after the test was over, and that timing, not fate, is what cost the deal.
